newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis arrested after seizing Hebron houses.
newsitem.headline: Israelis arrested after seizing Hebron houses.

text.p: Israeli troops scuffled with Jewish settlers on rooftops and in the streets of Hebron on Wednesday during protests against the expected handover of most of the West Bank town to Palestinian rule.

Witnesses said police arrested about 20 Jews in disturbances that began with the settlers' illegal pre-dawn takeover of two vacant houses in Hebron's Arab casbah. Soldiers and police removed the settlers from the houses.
Disturbances spread to the rooftops and the streets where settlers hurled eggs, apples and stones at soldiers, witnesses said. Israel Radio said a boy was injured.

Hebron's Jews are angry that a U.S.-brokered Israeli-PLO summit made progress on Tuesday towards a long-overdue Israeli transfer to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's Palestinian Authority of 80 percent of the volatile town holy to Moslems and Jews.

Witnesses said Palestinians were apparently behind two firebomb attacks near a Jewish home in Hebron and on an Israeli military border police vehicle later. No one was hurt but the car's roof was damaged.
The 400 settlers in the heart of the town of 100,000 Arabs fear Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu will risk their security if he signs the deal within a week as both sides predict.
Negotiating teams resumed talks in Jerusalem on Wednesday joined by U.S. special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross.
"We are not speaking of toppling the government. We are speaking of toppling the deal," Orit Struck, a Hebron settler woman, told Israeli army radio.

Hebron, taken by Israel with the rest of the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war, is the last Palestinian town due for self-rule under a 1995 peace deal. Israel's security fears have delayed its transfer.
"What's going on?" Palestinians asked when the disturbances began. "I'm afraid. I expect there will be a massacre," said Bassam Ahmaro, a 35-year-old Palestinian.
A settler from neighbouring Kiryat Arba enclave killed 29 Palestinian worshippers in 1994 in Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, known to Jews as the tomb of the biblical patriarch Abraham.

Hebron's settlers feel betrayed by Netanyahu, a rightist backer of Jewish settlement in occupied lands who has nonetheless promised to uphold the Hebron deal signed by the left-leaning government he ousted in May.
The Jews say they would expand their community but the government prevents them from buying property and limits them to building only in existing Jewish neighbourhoods.
"We'll not allow a violation of the law," Netanyahu's Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told Israel Radio.

Doubts the deal will improve on the security arrangements of the original accord have prompted criticism from Israeli coalition hardliners led by Infrastructure Minister Ariel Sharon, a former general.
The Arab casbah is in the 20 percent of Hebron due to remain under Israeli occupation in the deal along with Jewish enclaves.
The settlers said one house they took over was Jewish property and the other a building -- abutting a Jewish enclave -- that they fear the PLO will use to house guerrillas.
The fate of the Jews in Hebron and in other West Bank settlements will be decided in "final-status" talks between Israel and the Palestinians due to be completed by May 1999.
